title: CDC declares sprouts outbreak over — 77 sick in 16 states — but FDA won't name the seed supplier
excerpt: The CDC has declared an end to a dual E. coli and Salmonella outbreak traced to alfalfa sprouts that sickened at least 77 people in 16 states, with six hospitalizations and no deaths.
content:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has declared an end to a dual outbreak of E. coli and Salmonella traced to alfalfa sprouts and the seeds used to grow them — an outbreak that sickened at least 77 people in 16 states, with six hospitalizations and no deaths.

The outbreak was traced to Everything Sprouts of Minneapolis, Minnesota, and Berlin Seeds of Millersburg, Ohio. Both companies recalled their products. Sixty-four patients were infected with E. coli, 10 with Salmonella, and three with both. Illnesses began on dates ranging from May 31 to Oct. 19. Of the 52 patients interviewed, 41 reported eating sprouts before becoming ill.

The Food and Drug Administration closed its investigation on Nov. 9. The agency says it knows the name of the seed supplier behind the outbreak but has refused to publicly reveal it, reporting only the alfalfa seed lot SAL2-24JB, with an expiration date of Dec. 31, 2029. “Sprout growers should check their inventory for this recalled seed lot and discard any remaining seed,” the FDA said in its announcement.

The official count likely understates the toll: the CDC says that for every Salmonella patient identified in an outbreak, about 29 go undetected; for E. coli, about 26.

The CDC says anyone who ate the implicated sprouts or handled the implicated seeds and developed symptoms should seek medical attention and tell their doctor about the possible exposure, because specific tests are required to diagnose these infections. E. coli symptoms often include severe stomach cramps and diarrhea, which is often bloody, and sometimes fever. Salmonella symptoms can include diarrhea, abdominal cramps and fever within 12 to 72 hours after eating contaminated food.

Webb Watch flagged this outbreak in an Oct. 29 food-safety roundup; this story reports its closure — and the FDA's decision not to name the supplier.

Sources: Food Safety News, Nov. 10, 2026 (updated Nov. 11); CDC; FDA.
